opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. Right now, most of how our models learn vision is pretty passive. We show them enormous amounts of images and video paired with text, and they get very good at describing what's in a scene. But there's a real gap between being able to caption a photo and actually understanding the physical structure of the world: how objects occlude each other, what's behind something, how things would move if you pushed them, what's graspable, what's fragile.

Humans don't learn vision by staring at a fixed dataset. A baby is constantly reaching, moving their head, dropping things, putting things in their mouth. Vision gets grounded in action and consequence. You learn depth partly because you move and the world shifts in a consistent way. You learn object permanence because you hide something and then go find it. So the signal isn't just "what does this look like." It's "what happens when I do something."

So I think interaction could change things in a few ways. One is the data itself becomes self-supervised in a much richer way. If a model can take an action and observe the result, it gets a prediction target for free, and that's tied to causality, not just correlation in internet images. Another is active perception. Instead of being handed a single frame, the model can choose where to look, zoom in, change viewpoint, and resolve ambiguity itself. A lot of the failure modes we see today, like miscounting objects, getting spatial relations wrong, or misreading fine details, feel like things an agent that can look again would just fix.

And then there's the feedback loop. Once models are acting in the world, whether that's robotics or even just operating a computer through screenshots, you get very direct signal on whether their perception was right, because the action either works or it doesn't. That's a much sharper training signal than whether a caption roughly matches.

I don't want to overclaim. Real-world interaction is expensive, slow, and messy compared to scraping the internet, so I don't think it replaces large-scale pretraining. My guess is it looks more like pretraining giving you a strong prior, and interaction refining it into something that actually understands geometry and physics. But I do think that's where a lot of the remaining headroom in visual understanding is going to come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because the way we've trained vision models so far is kind of strange when you step back and look at it. We take a giant pile of images or video that someone else recorded, and the model just passively consumes it. It never gets to choose where to look. It never gets to ask, "What happens if I move this thing?" or "What's behind that object?" And that's not how any biological system learns to see.

The thing that changes when a model is actually interacting with the world is that it gets to generate its own training signal. If you push on an object and it moves, you just learned something about physics and about that object that no caption would have told you. If you walk around a chair, you get the 3D structure for free, with perfect consistency, because you know how you moved. A lot of the stuff we currently try to bake into models with clever losses or huge amounts of labeled data, like depth, permanence, affordances, what's rigid and what's deformable, all of that just falls out naturally when you have an embodied agent that can act and observe the consequences.

I think the other big shift is that vision stops being an end in itself and becomes something in service of a goal. Right now we evaluate vision models on, like, "Is this a dog?" But a robot doesn't actually care about classifying the dog. It cares about not stepping on the dog, or about grabbing the mug next to the dog. So the representations that emerge are going to be much more about what matters for acting than about what humans decided to label. And I suspect those representations end up being more robust, because they're grounded in whether the action actually worked, not in whether a human annotator agreed with you.

The honest caveat is that this is slow and expensive compared to scraping the internet. You can't just download a billion interactions. So I don't think it replaces the passive pretraining; I think it's the thing you do on top of it, where you take a model that already has a broad prior about how the world looks and then let it close the loop and correct all the places where that prior is subtly wrong. And there are a lot of those places. The gap between knowing what things look like and knowing how things behave is way bigger than most people appreciate until you put a model in a body and watch it fail.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift is going from observing the world to being able to test your understanding of it. If you’re learning from images or video, you see what happened, but you don’t necessarily know why it happened. When you can interact, you can push something, move around it, pick it up, and see whether the result matches what you expected.

Take an object sitting on a table. From an image, you might recognize what it is. But that doesn’t mean you understand how heavy it is, whether it’s attached to the table, or how it will move when you touch it. Acting gives you information that’s difficult to get from appearance alone.

So vision becomes part of a feedback loop: you perceive, make a prediction, act, and update your understanding. And the interesting possibility is that the model learns to choose actions specifically to resolve uncertainty. It moves to get a better view, or touches something to find out what it’s made of. That could lead to a much more grounded understanding of the physical world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift is going from observing the world to being able to test an understanding of it. If you learn vision from images, you see what things look like, but you don’t necessarily learn what happens when you interact with them. Can I pick this object up? Is it heavy? Does it move when I push it?

When a model can take an action and see the result, it gets a different kind of feedback. It can make a prediction, discover that it was wrong, and update its understanding. And it can choose another viewpoint or interaction to resolve uncertainty.

That makes vision part of a loop: perceive, act, observe, learn. The interesting question is whether that loop lets models develop a more useful understanding of the physical world with less data, because the data they’re collecting is directly connected to something they’re trying to do.
